titleEn: Roofer Down in a Heat Wave - Exertional Heat Stroke

patient.name: Tyler Brandt
patient.affectEn: restless and disoriented: moves restlessly on the tarp, pulls at his shirt, opens his eyes to your voice and follows simple commands only some of the time; flushed dark red and very hot
patient.speechEn: jumbled, inappropriate words ("Tuesday... shingles... I'm fine"); cannot give his own address or a coherent history - the two coworkers answer the history questions. After about 12 minutes of combined cooling (GCS 13) he is confused but can answer simple questions in short phrases.

scene.settingEn: Residential re-roofing job in Kelowna at 1505 hrs on the fourth day of a heat wave, 38 degrees C in the shade. The patient lies supine on a tarp in an open, shaded garage that is still very hot - about 33 degrees C inside. A ladder leans against the eaves and roofing debris is scattered on the driveway; the crew has stopped work. One patient, two coworkers with him; one coworker has a jug of ice water from the crew's cooler. Kelowna General Hospital is 14 minutes away; the nearest PCP car is 18 minutes out.
hazardsEn: ladder against the eaves - work has stopped
roofing debris on the driveway (trip hazard)
extreme heat - 38 degrees C outside, about 33 degrees C in the garage (this is the mechanism)

bystanders.knowsEn: They have been on the roof since 0700 with two short breaks, on the fourth day of the heat wave. He drank maybe one bottle of water all day and a large energy drink at lunch; half a sandwich at 1200 and nothing since. He complained of a headache and leg cramps at about 1300, seemed vague by 1400 and stopped sweating around 1400, then walked down the ladder and collapsed on the driveway at about 1455 - he did NOT fall. No seizure or shaking seen. No drugs or alcohol that he knows of. No medical problems that he knows of, not diabetic as far as he knows, no medications or supplements apart from the energy drink. Does not know about allergies. He is fit and works outdoors year round, no recent illness. Felt sick earlier but did not throw up, and has not been to pee all afternoon. Will help if told exactly what to do.

bystanders.who: second coworker (with the jug of ice water)
bystanders.knowsEn: Nothing beyond what the first coworker says. Has the crew's cooler with ice and a jug of ice water; can fetch it, soak towels or sheets, hold up a sheet for privacy, or help set up a basin of ice water for his feet and lower legs if he is asked. Gives the patient nothing to drink unless the candidate tells him to.

scene.partnerEn: one partner at your licence level; acts only on your delegation
equipmentEn: water, sheets and towels that can be soaked
the crew's cooler with ice and a jug of ice water (can be used for an improvised ice-water basin)
oxygen kit with non-rebreather mask and nasal cannula
PCP only: IV start kit with normal saline, D10W, acetaminophen and ibuprofen tablets

dispatchEn: 1505 hrs on the fourth day of a heat wave, 38 degrees C in the shade. Code 3 to a residential re-roofing job in Kelowna. A 34-year-old roofer has become confused and collapsed on the driveway. Coworkers have moved him into the shade of the garage. Kelowna General Hospital is 14 minutes away; the nearest PCP car is 18 minutes out.
dispatchUpdateEn: Dispatch adds: he has been on the roof since 0700 and stopped sweating about an hour ago according to a coworker. He is awake but 'talking nonsense'. Nobody saw him fall from any height - he walked down the ladder and collapsed on the driveway.
arrivalEn: A coworker waves you into the open garage. It is shaded but still very hot - about 33 degrees C inside. A ladder leans against the eaves and roofing debris is scattered across the driveway; the crew has stopped work. One patient on a tarp on the garage floor, two coworkers kneeling beside him. Your partner is right behind you with the kits.
firstLookEn: A young man lying on his back on a tarp in the shade of the garage, still in long pants, a long-sleeved shirt, boots and a hard hat. His skin is flushed dark red. He is moving restlessly and pulling at his shirt. Two coworkers are beside him; one is holding a jug of ice water.

primary.locEn: Awake but disoriented and restless: eyes open to your voice, pulls at his shirt, answers "Tuesday... shingles... I'm fine", cannot give his own address, obeys simple commands only some of the time. After about 12 minutes of combined cooling he is less restless and confused but answering simple questions.
primary.airwayEn: Patent, but it needs repositioning as he thrashes. No vomit or secretions at the moment; suction ready if needed.
primary.breathingEn: Respirations 30, shallow; clear air entry on both sides; equal chest rise.
primary.circulationEn: Radial pulse 138, weak, regular. No external bleeding.
primary.rbsEn: Rapid body survey: no head injury, no neck tenderness, moves all four limbs, no deformity, no bleeding - he did not fall from a height (he walked down the ladder and collapsed). Skin very hot to touch, flushed dark red, still slightly moist from earlier sweating (skin is given automatically during the RBS). He is still in long pants, a long-sleeved shirt, boots and a hard hat until the candidate removes them. Cooling, once started, is tolerated: no shivering.
primary.skinEn: very hot to touch, flushed dark red, slightly moist

history.ccEn: Patient: "I'm fine... shingles..." (jumbled words). Coworker: "He's been out of it - talking nonsense - and then he came down the ladder and just collapsed on the driveway."

opqrst.oEn: Coworker: "He said he had a headache and cramps around one o'clock, he was vague by two and stopped sweating around then, and he came down the ladder and collapsed on the driveway at about 1455, just before three."
opqrst.pEn: Coworker: "Nothing made it better. We just got him into the shade of the garage."
opqrst.qEn: Coworker: "He said he had a headache and his legs were cramping. Now he's just confused."
opqrst.rEn: Coworker: "I don't know. He never said."
opqrst.sEn: The patient cannot say. Coworker: "He didn't say how bad it was."
opqrst.tEn: Coworker: "Headache and cramps from about one, vague and not sweating from about two, down on the driveway since just before three."

history.painScoreEn: He cannot give a score (jumbled words); the coworkers know he complained of a headache and leg cramps at about 1300 but not how bad they were.

sample.sEn: Coworker: "Headache and leg cramps this afternoon, then he got confused, stopped sweating, and collapsed."
sample.aEn: Coworker: "No idea. I don't know if he's allergic to anything."
sample.mEn: Coworker: "Not that I know of. No supplements - just a big energy drink at lunch."
sample.pEn: Coworker: "Nothing I know of. He's healthy. Not diabetic as far as I know."
sample.lEn: Coworker: "Half a sandwich at noon. He drank maybe one bottle of water all day, plus the big energy drink at lunch."
sample.eEn: Coworker: "We've been on the roof since seven with two short breaks - fourth day of this heat wave. He's in long sleeves and long pants. He walked down the ladder and collapsed on the driveway - he didn't fall. No seizure, no shaking. No drugs or drinking that I know of."

fe.generalEn: Coworker: "He's fit - works outside all year. He hasn't been sick lately."
fe.cnsEn: Coworker: "Headache since about one, then confused and restless. No seizure that we saw."
fe.respiratoryEn: Coworker: "No cough. He wasn't short of breath that I noticed."
fe.cardiovascularEn: Coworker: "He never mentioned chest pain." (If his pulse or heart is asked about: his heart is racing.)
fe.giGuEn: Coworker: "He said he felt sick earlier but he didn't throw up. He hasn't gone to pee all afternoon."
fe.integumentaryEn: Dark red, flushed skin; sunburn on his forearms.
fe.musculoskeletalEn: Coworker: "His legs were cramping at about one."
fe.endocrineEn: Coworker: "He's not diabetic that we know of."

findings.headNeckEn: No injury from the collapse; mucous membranes very dry; no neck tenderness.
findings.chestLungsEn: Equal air entry at all six sites; no crackles.
findings.abdomenEn: Soft, non-tender in all four quadrants.
findings.backEn: Inspected during the transfer: no injury; skin hot everywhere.
findings.lowerExtremitiesEn: Calf muscles tight and tender from the cramps; pedal pulses weak but present; moves all limbs.
findings.upperExtremitiesEn: Sunburn on both forearms; weak radial pulses bilaterally; no tremor at rest.

vitalsSets.unlockNoteEn: baseline, taken while cooling is already running, completed in under 3 minutes; blood glucose is mandatory in this set (heat patient with a decreased LOC)
vitalsSets.skin: very hot, flushed dark red, slightly moist

vitalsSets.unlockNoteEn: en route, 8 minutes after set 1, after roughly 12 minutes of combined cooling - improving (temperature down 1.8 degrees); only unlocks once cooling has been started

expected.actionEn: Acknowledge and plan cooling equipment before arrival: cold packs, water, sheets or towels that can be soaked, the ambulance air conditioning set to maximum cold, oxygen, blood glucose meter and thermometer

Recognize the pattern from dispatch: prolonged exertion in extreme heat, altered mental status, and reported cessation of sweating - this is heat stroke until proven otherwise, and heat stroke is an unstable finding
triggers: altered mental status in the heat

expected.actionEn: Pre-cool the patient compartment on the way so the ambulance itself becomes a cooling tool on arrival

Verbalize hazards (ladder, roofing debris - work stopped), environment (extreme heat, this is the mechanism), nature of illness (heat illness after prolonged exertion), people (one patient plus two coworkers who can help cool him) and resources
Don gloves and eye protection
First look: young man, flushed dark red, restless and answering incorrectly, over-dressed for the conditions - start stripping the clothing as part of the first hands-on approach
Assess LOC / AVPU: awake but disoriented and restless - central nervous system dysfunction is what separates heat stroke from heat exhaustion
triggers: do you know where you are

expected.actionEn: Assess the airway and keep repositioning it as he thrashes; suction available
Assess breathing: 30 and shallow, auscultate both sides
Assess circulation: weak radial pulse of 138 - heat stroke produces a distributive and hypovolemic shock picture
Perform a full rapid body survey - a collapse on a work site still needs an injury sweep even when the cause looks medical
triggers: check for injuries from the collapse

expected.actionEn: Identify heat stroke as the life threat and begin cooling immediately as a primary survey intervention - rapid cooling is the indicated intervention for hyperthermia and it starts now, not after the secondary survey
Note the skin: very hot, flushed dark red, slightly moist
Oxygen for the altered LOC and shock picture, titrated to keep SpO2 at or above 94%
Position supine to support the blood pressure, out of the sun, with dignity maintained while the clothing comes off
Categorize as RTC out loud: heat stroke with an altered LOC
State and follow the timing rule: continue cooling for a minimum of 10 minutes before beginning conveyance, using that time for the history and the first set of vitals rather than standing still
triggers: cool for 10 minutes before we go

expected.actionEn: Continue the most aggressive available cooling during transport - the ambulance air conditioning on maximum cold plus soaked towels to head, torso and thighs
triggers: AC on max in the back

expected.actionEn: Do not delay departure to wait for the PCP car - cooling is the treatment and an EMR can deliver all of it
triggers: not waiting for the PCP car
we won't wait for the PCP

expected.actionEn: Establish the chief complaint: confusion and collapse after prolonged work in extreme heat
Take the HxC/C: hours of exposure and exertion, fluid intake, clothing, when symptoms started, when sweating stopped, whether anyone saw a fall or a seizure, and how long he has been down
triggers: how long has he been working
how much has he had to drink
how long has he been down

expected.actionEn: Ask about the earlier headache and cramps and score them - these were the warning signs of heat illness hours before the collapse
Past medical history from the coworkers, and document that it is second-hand
Medications and any supplements or stimulants, including the energy drink
Allergies - document as unknown rather than assuming none
Last oral intake, quantifying the fluid deficit across the shift
GCS with all three components stated separately
Blood pressure by auscultation
Pulse rate, rhythm and quality
Respiratory rate, depth and character with both lung fields auscultated
Skin assessed hands-on - and do not let the residual moisture talk you out of heat stroke
Pupils - size, equality and reaction
SpO2 recorded and monitored
Blood glucose - explicitly required in the initial vital signs of a heat patient with a decreased LOC
Temperature measured and repeated - it is the number that drives the cooling and the endpoint
FE - General health
FE - CNS (headache, confusion and restlessness define heat stroke rather than heat exhaustion)
FE - Respiratory
FE - Cardiovascular
FE - GI/GU (no urine output all afternoon quantifies the dehydration)
FE - Integumentary
FE - Musculoskeletal (the 1300 cramps were the first stage of heat illness)
FE - Endocrine
FE - EENT
Head and neck examined, including mucous membranes as a hydration marker
Chest auscultated at all six sites
Abdomen examined in four quadrants
Back examined during the transfer
triggers: look at his back during the transfer

expected.actionEn: Upper extremities with pulses and skin condition documented
Lower extremities with cramping muscles and pedal pulses documented
Move him to the coolest available area and remove all clothing, using a sheet to preserve dignity
triggers: move him to the coolest area

expected.actionEn: Apply cold wet towels to the head, torso and thighs and run convective cooling with the air conditioning on maximum cold, combining methods rather than using one alone
triggers: towels to the head torso and thighs

expected.actionEn: Improvise ice-water immersion of the feet and lower legs using the coworkers' cooler, and delegate the coworkers to help
triggers: feet and lower legs in ice water

expected.actionEn: Deliver a minimum of 10 minutes of cooling before beginning conveyance, and continue the most aggressive available cooling throughout transport
Withhold oral fluids and oral antipyretics: he cannot reliably protect his airway, and antipyretics do not lower temperature in heat stroke
Verbalize that intravenous fluid replacement is outside EMR scope and does not justify delaying cooling or transport
triggers: IV fluids are outside my scope
the hospital will give IV fluids
fluids are not in my scope

expected.actionEn: Reassess ABCs and interventions after each intervention and at least every 5 minutes
Second full set of vitals within 5-6 minutes with a repeat temperature, and interpret the falling temperature and improving GCS out loud
Keep cooling through transport and re-check the temperature repeatedly - improvement is not a reason to stop cooling
State the seizure plan: protect the airway, keep cooling, do not restrain the limbs, and reassess breathing afterwards
En-route notification of heat stroke with an altered LOC and active cooling
Complete verbal hand-off with the temperature trend and the cooling methods and duration
Accurate PCR completed within 5 minutes

specialEvents.descriptionEn: the candidate actually starts cooling the patient: removes his clothing, applies cold wet towels / soaked sheets, cold packs or ice water, immerses his feet and lower legs, or puts him in the cold air-conditioned ambulance (planning or pre-cooling the ambulance on the way is NOT this event)
the candidate cools him over his clothing, or leaves his shirt, pants or boots on instead of removing all clothing

before hospital arrival the candidate stops the cooling - removes the soaked towels / ice and does not replace them, turns the air conditioning off or down, or says cooling can stop because he is improving or talking sense. Briefly lifting towels for an exam or a transfer and re-applying them, or re-soaking them, is NOT this event.

the candidate begins conveyance (the ambulance leaves for hospital) before at least 10 minutes of cooling have been delivered - compare the transcript times of the departure and of the start of cooling. Loading him into the cold ambulance and continuing to cool there before driving is NOT this event.
the candidate delays departure on scene to wait for the PCP car after the 10 minutes of cooling have been delivered (asking for a PCP intercept en route is NOT this event)
the candidate gives, or lets a coworker give, the patient anything to drink by mouth (water, ice water, sports or energy drink). Pouring or sponging water OVER him to cool him is NOT this event.
the candidate lets or asks the patient to stand up or walk (e.g. to the ambulance or the cot)

drugs.doseEn: 500-1000 mg PO (PCP) - WITHHELD in this call: antipyretics do not lower the temperature in heat stroke (the problem is heat load, not a raised set point) and he cannot reliably protect his airway (if given, record drug:acetaminophen)
300-400 mg PO (PCP) - WITHHELD in this call: antipyretics do not lower the temperature in heat stroke and he cannot reliably protect his airway (if given, record drug:ibuprofen)

15 g PO for BGL below 4.0 mmol/L only in a patient with sufficient mentation to maintain his airway - NOT indicated: BGL is 5.1 mmol/L and his mentation is insufficient (if given, record drug:oral-glucose)
for hypoglycemia (BGL below 4.0 mmol/L) with insufficient mentation - NOT indicated: BGL is 5.1 mmol/L (if given, record drug:glucagon)
PCP: 10-25 g (100-250 mL of 10% solution) IV for confirmed hypoglycemia - NOT indicated: BGL is 5.1 mmol/L (if given, record drug:d10w)

PCP only: IV fluid replacement for the signs and symptoms of dehydration (no urine all afternoon, dry mucous membranes, weak pulse 138, BP 96/54), started en route without slowing the cooling; outside EMR scope

examinerPrompts.locNotDepictedEn: He opens his eyes to your voice, is restless and disoriented, says jumbled words and follows simple commands only some of the time.
examinerPrompts.breathingNotDepictedEn: He is breathing fast and shallow.

trackNotes.emrEn: Every element of definitive prehospital care here is EMR-level: recognition of heat stroke by exposure plus central nervous system dysfunction, moving him to the coolest area, complete undressing with dignity preserved, combined evaporative and convective cooling with soaked towels to head, torso and thighs plus maximum-cold air conditioning, improvised ice-water immersion of the feet and lower legs, a minimum of 10 minutes of cooling before conveyance with cooling continued all the way in, oxygen to 94% or above, supine positioning, airway watch with suction, a mandatory blood glucose, and repeated temperatures. Only intravenous fluid replacement sits outside EMR scope. No oral fluids, no oral antipyretics, no glucose (BGL 5.1). Do not wait on scene for the PCP car once the 10 minutes of cooling have been delivered.
trackNotes.pcpEn: PCP adds the 9-system Functional Enquiry and considers fluid replacement for the signs and symptoms of dehydration - no urine output all afternoon, dry mucous membranes and a weak pulse of 138 after a shift with roughly one bottle of water. Cooling remains the priority and is identical at both levels; fluids are given en route without slowing the cooling. Antipyretics (acetaminophen, ibuprofen) are withheld; D10W and glucagon are not indicated (BGL 5.1).

sourcePages: Scenario emd-06 (data/practical/emr-medical-1.json): dispatch, scene, primary (cooling as a primary-survey intervention), transport (RTC; minimum 10 minutes of cooling before conveyance; keep cooling en route), history from coworkers, vitals sets 1-2, FE, exam, interventions, ongoing (seizure plan), handoff, critical pitfalls. BC Provincial Examination Guidelines (current to June 15, 2026): p.7 Findings in Unstable Adult Patients (altered LOC; heat stroke); p.11 Primary survey intervention indications (rapid cooling for hyperthermia; oxygen for altered LOC and evidence of shock; airway maintenance and suctioning for decreased LOC); p.36 Heat Exhaustion/Heatstroke (move to a cool area; remove all clothing; convective cooling with AC on maximum cold; cold wet towels to head, torso and thighs; immersion of feet and legs in ice water; minimum 10 minutes of cooling before conveyance; blood glucose in the initial vitals if decreased LOC; most aggressive cooling during transport; PCP: consider fluid replacement for dehydration); p.50 Oxygen Administration (titrate to SpO2 94%); p.57 Diabetic Emergencies (BGL in the baseline vitals; correct hypoglycemia below 4.0 mmol/L); p.58 Acetaminophen; p.61 D10W; p.67 Glucagon; p.68 Ibuprofen; p.76 Oral Glucose (only with sufficient mentation to maintain an airway).
